cards.title: Automate influencer sourcing and outreach to scale partnership ads
cards.summary: Use AI to automate the find, screen, outreach and media-kit negotiation steps of influencer marketing so you can multiply conversations per week without adding headcount.
cards.use_when: Planning influencer/partnership ad acquisition and trying to increase creator volume for TikTok/Meta partnership ads.
steps: Map the current manual workflow end to end: source/screen creators against a written brand-fit brief, outreach, request media kit, negotiate a rebuttal to the quoted rate, and offer a performance kicker if it performs.

Automate the repetitive stages with AI while keeping the brand-fit judgment human: the presenter argues the person screening must effectively be the customer to understand the audience, and says a head of influence for one brand would not do a good job for a different brand.
Set volume targets: the presenter scaled from ~500 real creator conversations per week (creators with 100k+ audience) to 200–300 per day after automating, with a goal of 500 per day.
Treat it as a one-time build plus ongoing optimization rather than a variable opex problem.
Keep the negotiation logic explicit: counter the media kit rate with a stated CPM baseline and offer a kicker if performance is strong.
caveats: Results are the presenter's own example, not a benchmark; exact conversation volume depends on niche and team.
The presenter concedes AI UGC creators are not there yet for his scale (quality and legality), so he automates the process, not the creator itself.
Verify current AI tooling and platform rules before building.

cards.title: Back a human-first creative thesis while hedging on AI ads
cards.summary: The presenter bets platforms will reward real-human partnership ads over AI slop, but flags regulation and unclear platform incentives as real risks.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate creative budget between human influencer/partnership ads and AI-generated statics/video.
steps: Use AI-generated static ads freely: the presenter says all his statics are now AI, while continuing to invest in human creators for video.

Lean budget into partnership ads and TikTok influencers because, in a market commoditized by Amazon and AI, the presenter argues people want to buy from real humans and platforms will reward real people in-feed.
Hedge: acknowledge the opposing possibility that platforms will simply push whatever AI ads perform better for them regardless of 'human' sentiment.
Track regulatory developments: the presenter notes New York banned AI UGC ads with fines, as an opposing force to AI creative growth.
Treat AI-video parity with human UGC as a matter of when, not if, and re-test periodically rather than committing permanently.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated opinion/bet, not a proven rule.
Predictions about platform behavior and timelines are explicitly uncertain (the other speaker predicted 30–50% AI video by end of next year; presenter declined to commit).

cards.title: Localize pricing, language and merchandising to unlock non-US revenue
cards.summary: Model localization on a best-in-class case: per-market languages, localized pricing, and market-specific merchandising, not just one translated site.
cards.use_when: Expanding a DTC store into international markets or improving conversion in existing non-US traffic.
steps: Study a strong localizer as a reference: the presenter cites Caseify (phone cases) as localizing languages, pricing and even merchandising per market (UK vs China vs Korea, e.g. region-relevant collab/character cases).
Go beyond translated copy: the presenter says for a brand big in Asia the site should use Asian models and local languages (Chinese, Thai, Vietnamese) matching the countries shipped to.
Localize pricing per market rather than converting one currency blindly.
Note the presenter's own varied international mix (roughly 60% US/Canada, 40% non-North America; one brand ~35% US, 65% non-US) as context for why localization scales.
Treat localization as a distinct operating capability, not a one-off translation project.
caveats: The presenter says his own team is currently bad at localization, so treat this as a target state, not a described proven process.
Named companies are referenced as examples, not guaranteed benchmarks.

cards.title: Level 1 international shipping: one 3PL, one global campaign, best creatives
cards.summary: A simple first step for cross-border: house light inventory in a Hong Kong 3PL and run one Meta campaign with all best-performing North America creatives against every shippable country.
cards.use_when: Starting international expansion for a light-product store (e.g. phone cases, small electronics) with limited operational resources.
steps: If the product is small/light, store inventory with a Hong Kong 3PL and ship out of there; the presenter calls this simple and fast for light goods.
Run one new global Meta campaign with one ad set, loading it with all your best-performing North America creatives.
Include all countries you can physically ship to at a reasonable price in that single ad set.
Run ads in English to start; localize language/imagery later as a second optimization level.
Then optimize variable costs (shipping and fulfillment) as the 'level one' cost unlock for international markets.
caveats: Applies most cleanly to light products; heavier or bulky goods need different logistics.
The presenter notes even US-fulfilled orders can sometimes ship cheaper from Hong Kong via a cross-border logistics provider, delivering in ~4.5 days on average in his example.

cards.title: Cross-border logistics can beat domestic fulfillment on cost and speed
cards.summary: A cross-border provider that dropships from Asia to US customers in under 5 days can be cheaper than domestic end-to-end fulfillment.
cards.use_when: Evaluating fulfillment options or trying to reduce shipping cost and delivery time for a US-facing store.
steps: Compare total landed cost of domestic 3PL/fulfillment versus shipping direct from an Asia-based cross-border provider for your specific SKUs and volumes.

Use the presenter's data point as a hypothesis to test: he says it is cheaper for him to ship US orders from Hong Kong via Quinc Logistics than to fulfill end-to-end inside the US, averaging ~4.5 days to a US customer.
Look for providers that built internal infrastructure to consolidate dropship from China, India and Asia into fast, cheap US delivery.
If a provider externalizes this capability to other brands, treat it as a sourcing lever to negotiate.
caveats: Specific costs and delivery times are the presenter's example, not a benchmark; terms vary and should be verified with current providers.
Brand facts about named companies should be checked before relying on them.

cards.title: Build a daily red/green/blue P&L report with mandatory explanations
cards.summary: Automate a daily Slack report of revenue, spend and key metrics with color status, and require the responsible owner to explain every miss in-thread.
cards.use_when: Setting up operating cadence and accountability for an ecommerce P&L.
steps: Produce a daily Slack update (AI-generated in the presenter's case, previously via virtual assistants) showing budgeted vs actual for revenue, ad spend, ROAS, repeat rate and other P&L lines by day.
Use color codes: e.g. one color for miss vs budget, another for beat, another for off-forecast; the presenter uses red/green/blue.
Publish to a town-hall-style channel everyone can see.
Require the accountable owner to reply in-thread whenever a metric is red, explaining why and the corrective plan (an SOP exists for each color).
If the same metric is off-forecast repeatedly (the presenter says many blue lights three days in a row), require an explanation of why the budget/forecast was so wrong to begin with.
caveats: Compounding small daily improvements is the presenter's motivating rationale, not a measured guarantee.
He notes he has not yet applied AI to the per-person reporting layer out of respect for individuals.

cards.title: Run a daily task channel with every direct report
cards.summary: Each team member posts a morning plan and end-of-day completion plus time allocation, letting a leader spot overload and misplaced effort.
cards.use_when: Managing an ecommerce team's productivity and diagnosing why a channel (e.g. PPC) is missing targets.
steps: Create a personal daily-task channel per team member; the presenter has ~70 such channels for his front-office staff.
Each morning the person posts the 3 things they want to accomplish today plus the rest of their to-do list.
Each evening they post what got done (with check marks) and a breakdown of how time was spent (e.g. 30 min email, 1 hour Meta ad manager, 30 min Google ad manager).
Use the time-allocation logs to decide whether someone needs support, is overloaded, or is spending time on non-impactful work.
Cross-reference the individual channel with the macro P&L channel: if PPC metrics are red, check whether the owner is under-investing hours in creative production.
Use the accumulated logs as a factual basis for six-month reviews instead of relying on memory.
caveats: High-intensity, hands-on management style; the presenter frames it as a deliberate choice, not a fit for every manager or team.
Requires consistent participation to be useful.

cards.title: Reframe micromanagement as structured recurring feedback
cards.summary: The presenter says micromanagement fails only when it is unprompted, random and unstructured; make it predictable, daily and consistent to train juniors.
cards.use_when: Onboarding or developing junior ecommerce operators and deciding whether/how closely to manage them.
steps: Give feedback at a predictable, consistent daily frequency rather than randomly.
Make the feedback structured and expected, so the recipient knows when and how it will come.
Pair frequent feedback with a system (daily P&L colors, daily task channels) so the leader is 'in the weeds' without being bogged down.
Lead by example: the presenter says leaders should also solicit and accept feedback, and participate in the same systems.
Hire for attitude toward feedback: filter for people who treat feedback as a gift and who are self-deprecating rather than defensive.
caveats: This is the presenter's explicitly contrarian opinion ('micromanaging is a great word'); it is a strong style choice, not a universal best practice.
The pattern is presented as training-focused, most relevant to junior employees.

cards.title: Adopt the A Method's five-step hiring sequence
cards.summary: Scorecard, screening, topgrading, competency/culture, then reference-checked offer — a standardized sequence that made hiring comparable and durable.
cards.use_when: Building out an ecommerce team (e.g. head of finance or other key hires) and wanting a repeatable process to reduce early attrition.
steps: Step 1 — Scorecard: define outcomes and the specific attributes/competencies the role truly needs (and what it does NOT need, e.g. a head of finance does not need to be charismatic or extroverted).
Step 2 — Screening: a standardized, role-agnostic 15–20 minute set of macro questions any recruiter can run, with maniacal notes passed to the hiring manager.
Step 3 — Topgrading: a 30–60 minute deep, chronological walk through each résumé role, filling gaps (e.g. what happened between two jobs) and chasing flagged concerns.
Step 4 — Competency and culture: a domain case study (often with dummy data and deliberate traps) plus a cultural-fit questionnaire (e.g. comfort with constant feedback).
Step 5 — Reference-checked offer: make the offer conditional on 2–3 reference calls for senior hires, asking standardized questions tied to what screening/topgrading surfaced to get past fluff.
Keep a straight line through the doc: everything should reconcile, with no zigs or zags.
caveats: The presenter credits this method (plus learning from a near-bankruptcy) as central to scaling from ~$50M to $200M; that is his own case, not a proven benchmark.
He says reference calls are worthless for most people unless run through this standardized process.

cards.title: Write a role scorecard that separates outcomes from attributes
cards.summary: Define what the role must deliver and the specific competences/attributes needed, and explicitly list what does not matter to remove interviewer bias.
cards.use_when: Writing a job description or evaluating candidates for an ecommerce role (e.g. head of finance).
steps: List concrete outcomes (e.g. build financial models, produce management accounts, run audits, budgeting, monitoring and risk).
List the real competencies (e.g. extreme attention to detail/OCD, strong analytical skills, decent problem solving, a get-it-done hands-on attitude).

Explicitly name irrelevant traits to avoid bias: the presenter says for head of finance he does not need charisma, extroversion or someone who excites him in the interview — he wants the boxes ticked.
Use the scorecard to align everyone involved in hiring (hiring manager, CEO, future manager) before interviewing.
In the screening, test career goals against the role's growth path (e.g. an aspiring CFO fits a head-of-finance stepping-stone hire; someone who wants to coast is a bad fit).
caveats: Some competency specifics (extreme OCD) may vary by company, though the presenter says head-of-finance competencies are largely consistent across companies.
Bias-removal is the goal; results depend on disciplined use.

cards.title: Use screening booby-trap questions to test fit and flag deep-dive topics
cards.summary: A short standardized screen with deliberately probing questions surfaces fit and generates hypotheses to drill into during topgrading.
cards.use_when: Running first-round screens for any ecommerce role and deciding who advances.
steps: Ask one question from each core area: what are your career goals; what are you really good at professionally; what are you not good at professionally; who were your last five managers and how would they rate you 1–10; and why do you want to work here.
For the rating question, use the framing 'if I called [manager] and asked him to rate you 1–10, how would he rate you?' and probe 'why an 8 and not a 9' to get past polite answers.
Note red flags but don't resolve them in screening — carry them forward. Example: a candidate citing lateness on deliverables gets a note to probe prioritization in topgrading.
Use role-specific deal-breakers: for head of finance, disliking repetitive process work is a disqualifier because closing the books must be owned by this person.
Leave ~10 minutes at the end for the candidate's questions and always sell the company, even if you plan to reject, so the candidate leaves excited.
caveats: Screening alone does not resolve the flags it surfaces; that is topgrading's job.
The 'always be selling' closing is a nuance the presenter adds beyond the book, based on his own experience.

cards.title: Topgrade candidates chronologically to find gaps and inflated titles
cards.summary: Walk every résumé role in order to verify what someone was actually hired to do versus their title, and to fill timeline gaps.
cards.use_when: Second-stage interviews where you need to verify a candidate's real track record before an ecommerce hire.
steps: Go role by role through the CV rather than accepting the summary.
Distinguish hired-title from final-title: the presenter's own example — hired as entrepreneur-in-residence, left as managing director — and ask what it actually took to progress.
Ask what the person was actually hired to do, what they did, and what results they drove in each role.
Probe chronological gaps: the presenter looks for holes (e.g. what were you doing between these two jobs, what went wrong).
Allocate 30–60 minutes for this stage, deeper than the 15–20 minute screen.
caveats: Takes real time per candidate; best reserved for those who passed screening.
Effectiveness depends on the interviewer's domain knowledge to judge the answers.

cards.title: Use case studies with traps plus a culture questionnaire
cards.summary: Test domain competence with a realistic exercise containing deliberate traps, then check cultural fit against your actual operating system.
cards.use_when: Final-stage evaluation of an ecommerce hire, especially specialized roles like finance or growth.
steps: Build a role-specific case study: e.g. for head of finance, spotting mistakes in management accounts and reconciling the income statement against the balance sheet.
Embed deliberate traps and use dummy/fake data so you can test attention to detail and analytical skill without exposing real data.
Have candidates sign a mutual NDA if you give access to real materials.
Follow with a cultural-fit questionnaire asking directly about your operating norms: are they okay with constant feedback, with giving you constant feedback, and with the daily Slack system.
Lead by example on culture: the presenter says he participates in the same daily task channel he asks employees to use.
caveats: Culture questions only work if you are honest about the real norms; mismatches cause early attrition.
Traps must be fair and role-relevant to be valid signals.

cards.title: Cut packaging cost and lift LTV with a bill of materials
cards.summary: Packaging spend hides in 'dummy numbers'; building a proper bill of materials exposes waste and packaging upgrades can raise LTV.
cards.use_when: Reviewing COGS/packaging for a DTC brand or sourcing better packaging suppliers.
steps: Build a real bill of materials for your product instead of treating packaging as an assumed lump figure; the presenter says mentees cut packaging cost by more than 50% once they had a BOM.
Use the BOM to benchmark what each packaging component actually should cost rather than what you currently pay.
Consider packaging quality as a lever on customer experience: the presenter says upgrading packaging at one brand correlated with ~15% higher LTV.
If packaging is a pain point, look at whether a specialized packaging supplier (the presenter launched one for this reason) offers better pricing and process.
Treat packaging as a low-risk, high-return first step before broader sourcing overhaul.
caveats: The 15% LTV lift and 50% cost cuts are the presenter's examples, not guaranteed outcomes; verify with your own data.
Named supplier is the presenter's own venture.

cards.title: Automate procurement from weekly to daily purchase orders
cards.summary: At thousands of SKUs, custom software can move PO placement from weekly to daily with consistent logic, improving replenishment responsiveness.
cards.use_when: Managing replenishment and purchase orders for a high-SKU ecommerce catalog.
steps: Recognize the operational constraint: with thousands of SKUs, weekly PO cycles are hard to run well manually; the presenter built custom software to place POs daily.
Encode replenishment logic in the system so daily POs follow rules rather than manual judgment each time.
Treat this as a build-once system (the presenter's team built it for themselves) rather than a per-cycle cost.
Look ahead to agentic supply chain: the presenter's goal is an AI agent that talks to supplier agents and places orders automatically based on real sell-through volume.
caveats: Requires development resources; the presenter built custom software for his own business.
The agent-to-agent vision is a stated future goal, not a described working system yet.

cards.title: Evaluate your business for picks-and-shovels spin-offs
cards.summary: Operators with proven internal capabilities (packaging, logistics, supply-chain software) can productize them for other brands as a new revenue line.
cards.use_when: Considering new revenue streams or evaluating whether an internal capability could serve other ecommerce brands.
steps: Identify capabilities you built for yourself that other brands struggle with — the presenter's examples: packaging (Petra Sparks), cross-border logistics, and supply-chain automation.
Validate demand from peers/mentees before investing; the presenter saw mentees overpaying for packaging, then launched a supplier.
Deliver clear value (cost savings) so the win is two-sided, mirroring a good supplier relationship.
Consider whether an 'agentic layer' on top (e.g. agent-to-agent ordering against real sell-through) is a differentiation others lack.
Use external visibility (content) to generate demand: the presenter reported building a $150M ARR pipeline of interest for a logistics service by posting.
caveats: Pipeline figures are interest/analyzed spend, not booked revenue.
Productizing internal tools may be premature while they still generate too much internal value.

cards.title: Build personal-brand content to generate deal flow, not just audience
cards.summary: Treat content as a deliberate pipeline channel for deals, partnerships and advisory opportunities rather than a vanity metric.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether/how to invest in founder content for sourcing deals, suppliers or partnerships.
steps: Set the explicit goal as deal flow: the presenter built his personal brand because he felt obligated to generate returns for external shareholders and needed to source deals.
Pick a platform that fits your output style (he chose X/Twitter for written content, despite not being a big Twitter user).
Even a small following can work if it is the right audience — he built a $150M ARR interest pipeline from ~16,000 followers by talking about cost-saving services.
Use content to help other founders save money or get better offers, creating reciprocal goodwill and inbound.
Maintain the channel even when not actively buying/acquiring, because it compounds into community, events and advisory roles.
caveats: Pipeline/interest figures are not booked revenue.
Audience size is not the goal; relevance to sourcing and partnerships is.

cards.title: Check numbers daily, with a light weekend rule
cards.summary: Run the business like a bakery — count the buns and the cash every day — but consider explicitly pausing on weekends.
cards.use_when: Setting the leader's own operating rhythm for monitoring an ecommerce P&L.
steps: Adopt a daily numbers habit: the presenter credits a Rocket Internet mentor's 'we're bakers' metaphor — buy flour, bake, sell, count unsold buns and cash every day.
Automate and simplify the daily check (e.g. to a three-color Slack digest) so being in the weeds does not bog you down.
Do not delegate the habit of personally looking at the numbers fully to AI; the presenter wants a digest to assist but keeps the personal habit.
If you want a break, define it explicitly: the presenter does not check numbers on weekends and scrolls analytics only lightly.
Reserve deep-work time for the highest-leverage problems (the presenter cites ~2–3 hours of concentrated work plus ~2 hours of communication a day, focused on moonshots).
caveats: The specific workday hours are the presenter's personal setup, not a prescription.
Daily checking is a personal discipline that may not suit every manager.
